a, Unsupervised classification of sSC using the standard fresh-frozen MERFISH protocol. UMAP embedding of 5,845 cells reveals consistent clustering of the same 8 ENCs and 11 INCs identified with TransA-MERFISH on fixed tissue (Fig. 1d). Cell-type labels were assigned to Leiden clusters based on canonical marker gene expression patterns and transcriptomic mapping via a supervised XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH atlas. b, Confusion matrix showing transcriptomic correspondence between cell types in standard MERFISH (rows) and TransA-MERFISH (columns). c, Violin plots comparing quality control metrics between standard MERFISH (blue) and TransA-MERFISH (gray). Distributions are highly similar across key metrics, including the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts), total transcript counts per cell (total_counts), and cell mask area (in pixels). A modest reduction in n_genes_by_counts and total_counts was observed in TransA-MERFISH experiments. d, Comparison of matched neuronal subtype frequencies between standard MERFISH and TransA-MERFISH. Values are plotted on a ln-ln scale to highlight low-frequency types. A strong correlation is observed across both excitatory and inhibitory populations, indicating that the TransA-MERFISH protocol did not bias or deplete neuron types in the sSC (Pearson R = 0.88). e, Validation accuracies of the XGBoost classifier trained using various gene selection strategies: the performance of the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel was compared to randomly sampled 140-gene sets drawn from either the full single-cell transcriptome or the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs). Additional gene sets were constructed by selecting the top k specific genes (Methods) per SC neuronal cluster (k = 1–10), based on 19 neuronal clusters identified from re-clustering of the neuronal subset of the dataset28. Data are presented as mean ± SD. f, Dot plots comparing the expression patterns of 2 non-optimal probes (top row, blue) with their corresponding expressions in snRNA-seq17 (bottom row, orange). MERFISH cells are grouped according to their predicted snRNA-seq cluster identities, as inferred by Tangram-based imputation (Methods). The 140-gene list is presented in Supplementary Table 1. g-j, Classification and filtering of non-neuron cells (NNs). UMAP embedding (g) of all high-quality cells (47740 cells after quality filtering, see Methods) before filtering out non-neuronal cells, colored by broad cell classes: excitatory neurons (ENCs), inhibitory neurons (INCs), and NNs. NNs were identified using a supervised XGBoost classifier (i) trained on an SC snRNA-seq dataset, as in the reference28. Violin plots (h) of quality control metrics show that NNs exhibit reduced numbers of detected genes per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts per cell (total_counts), consistent with the design principles for neurons in the TransA-MERFISH gene panel. Bar plots (j) showing the average proportions of ENCs and INCs among all detected cells across animals. NNs were subsequently filtered out before re-clustering of neuronal cells to improve classification resolution among neuronal types. n = 16 animals. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

a,b, Transcriptomic correspondence between the MERFISH-based sSC neuron atlas and the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (CCN20230722; Allen Institute)20. (a) UMAP embedding of the TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), colored by the most probable mapped supertype identity inferred via MapMyCells. (b) Confusion matrix showing the correspondence between TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (rows) and 10 x WMB supertypes (columns), as determined by MapMyCells mapping (Methods). c, Transcriptomic correspondence between the TransA-MERFISH sSC neuron atlas and the Trans-Seq single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) SC neuron atlas9, as determined by XGBoost-based classification (Methods). Dot size and color represent the proportion of cells from each Trans-Seq cluster (y-axis) mapped to the corresponding TransA-MERFISH neuronal types (x-axis), indicating the scRNA-seq-based protocol biases a few neuronal subsets due to the nature of the dissociation and FACS sorting, thus it is not optimal to represent adult neuron clusters precisely and comprehensively. d, Dot plot comparing transcriptomic signatures of representative neuronal types across three datasets: TransA-MERFISH (red), single-nucleus RNA-seq (green)22, and supertypes from the 10x Genomics-based Whole Mouse Brain (WMB) taxonomy (blue; corresponding to panels a,b). Shown are selected excitatory neuron types—including Cdh7+ SC neurons (ENC1, ENC2), Npnt+ wide-field SC neurons (ENC5), and Etv1+ SC neurons (ENC6)—as well as inhibitory neuron types, including Cbln4+ SC neurons (INC1) and Fibcd1+ SC neurons (INC3). The consistent expression patterns of key marker genes across datasets support the robustness of cell classification in the TransA-MERFISH atlas and align with mapping results obtained via machine learning (g,j) and MapMyCells (a,b). e-j, Alignments of the TransA-MERFISH neuronal clusters with past single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-Seq) atlases of the mouse SC, indicating consistency across datasets. Re-clustering of neuronal subsets from reference datasets reproduced the original cell-type assignments (e17 and h22). Confusion matrices (f,i) show that XGBoost models trained on the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel achieve high validation accuracy in recovering snRNA-seq-defined cell types. Heatmaps (g,j) show the transcriptomic correspondence between snRNA-seq cell clusters (y-axis) and the TransA-MERFISH types (x-axis), based on predictions from an XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH dataset using the 140 genes. Color intensity reflects the percentage of cells from each snRNA-seq cluster mapped to each TransA-MERFISH type.

a-b, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with cells colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (a), and split UMAP embedding for each replicate separately (b), showing consistent cluster structure across replicates. c, Histograms display consistent percentages of neurons for each dataset contributing to each identified neuron type, for a stable representation of cell types across datasets. d, Violin plots showing the distributions of the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts) and total transcripts detected per cell (total counts) across each of the 19 sSC neuronal types. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. f, UMAP embedding of TransA-MERFISH neuron atlas (Fig. 1d), with mWmC+ neurons colored by individual dataset identities corresponding to each reaction (as in panel a). g, UMAP distribution for each of the three datasets separately, showing that all mWmC+ types have contributions from three reactions. e, Stacked barplot shows consistent mWmC+ labeling of each retino-recipient neuron type across datasets, ensuring a stable representation of retino-recipient cell types. h, Bar plots showing the proportions of each cell type across the three replicates. Comparisons across tracing conditions using the Kruskal–Wallis test revealed no differences among cell types (p > 0.05). Data are presented as mean ± SD. i, left, Example of raw MERFISH images with DAPI (gray) and RNA transcripts (blue); colored segmented cell masks are generated using a customized Cellpose 2.0 model. middle, Similar to (left) but overlapped with curated colored masks annotated manually as a benchmark. right, Comparison of Cellpose model-generated masks and curated masks. Light green shows true positive (TP), pink show False Positive (FP), and purple show False Negative (FN). j, Violin plot showing the performance score across three animals. Calculation of precision, recall and F1 are as following: Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN), F1 = 2 * Precision * Recall / (Precision + Recall). The horizontal line within the violin indicates the median. k, Violin plot showing the distribution of Intersection over Union (IoU) across animals and images. Violin plots show the distribution of the data. The centre line indicates the median, and the lower and upper bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, respectively.

a-e, Consistent dorsal-ventral cluster distribution along the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral axes. Sample images (a) showing the spatial distribution of cell clusters within each slice across the anterior-posterior axis. Compositional distribution of different neuron clusters (b, excitatory; c, inhibitory) across the anterior-to-posterior axis. Compositional distribution of different neuronal clusters (d, excitatory; e, inhibitory) along the medial-to-lateral axis. n = 16 animals. f-g, Sample images showing sublaminar distribution for each ENC (f) or INC (g) along the dorsal-ventral axis of the sSC. The somata median positions along the dorsal-ventral axis are plotted for all ENC and INC (Fig. 1f). Colored lines are the mean; gray lines are individual measurements. Scale bars, 100 μm.

a, Schematic of strategy to examine selective connectivity from all RGCs (AAV2-ChR2-YFP, green) to SC neurons (either SC-FlpO; FSF-RFP or SC-Cre; FSF-RFP, red) using CRACM. b-d, CRACM experiments show findings consistent with those from TransA-MERFISH, in which RGCs innervate ENC5 (Npnt+, b) but not ENC6 (Etv1+, c). Amplitudes of evoked currents and percentages of innervations were quantified in (d). n = 4 animals; 7 out of 13 ENC5 were connected, 2 out of 9 ENC6 were weakly innervated. *p = 0.0478, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. e-h, Experimental scheme (e) for findings in (Fig. 1k) using immunohistochemistry shows co-staining with anti-RFP and anti-Npnt antibodies (f,h, n = 4 animals; 128 neurons), whereas no co-localization was observed between goat anti-RFP and rabbit anti-Etv1 antibodies (g,h, n = 4 animals; 103 neurons). (h) Statistical results for f,g. Scale bar, 20 μm. ***p = 0.0004, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. i, Comparison of the frequencies of labeled Npnt+ wide-field neurons among vGlut2+ neurons within the regions used for MERFISH analysis and replot of the percentage of Npnt+ SC neurons from Liu et al. n = 4 animals. n.s. not significant. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. ***p = 0.0002, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. j-k, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in ENC1 and ENC2 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Cdh7 (red) is enriched in Cdh7-FlpO; FSF-Stop-GFP (Cdh7-GFP, green), indicating correspondence to ENC1 and ENC2 neuron clusters (j), as quantified in (k). Dotted yellow circles indicate in situ signals that overlap with GFP staining. n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars, 50 μm. l-m, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in INC1 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Cbln4 (red) is enriched in Cbln4-FlpO; FSF-Stop-GFP (Cbln4-GFP, green), indicating correspondence to the INC1 neuron cluster (l) as quantified in (m). Dotted yellow circles indicate in situ signals that overlap with GFP staining. n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars: 50 μm. n-o, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in INC1 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Cbln4 expression (red) is exclusive of Cdh7-GFP (green) (n), as quantified in (o). n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars, 50 μm. p-q, Validation of TransA-MERFISH marker gene expression in ENC1 and ENC2 using RNA-Scope in situ hybridization. Itga7 (red, ENC1) and Sntb1 (blue, ENC2) are mutually exclusive in Cdh7-GFP SC neurons (p), as quantified in (q). ENC1 and ENC2 each account for 50% and 25% of the total GFP neurons, respectively, while neither Itga7 nor Sntb1 overlaps. n = 4 biologically independent animals. Scale bars, 50 μm. All data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. Schematics in a,e adapted from ref. 6, Springer Nature.

a, AAV vector design for Pan mWGA-mCherry (AAV2-CAG-mWmC-WPRE) and Cre-dependent mWGA-mCherry (AAV2-CAG-DIO-mWmC-WPRE) expression to achieve neuronal subtype-specific anterograde transsynaptic tracing. RGC percentage is quantified on the right. Scale bar, 20 μm. n = 3 biologically independent animals. b-d, mWGA-mCherry expressed in Foxp2+ RGCs. Foxp2-cre is a driver for the F-RGC subclass (Foxp2-positive, b) but distinct from Spp1, a marker for αRGCs (c), as quantified in (d). n = 3 biologically independent animals e-h, mWGA-mCherry expressed in Tusc5+ RGCs. Tusc5-cre is a driver for the T5-RGC subclass (Tusc5+, (e) but is distinct from Spp1 (f) and partially overlaps with Foxp2 (g), as quantified in (h). n = 4 biologically independent animals i, Normalized GFP axon fluorescence intensity of line scans drawn perpendicular to the SC pia surface (solid line is mean intensity curve; light lines are each example; shadows are s.e.m.) across four different genotypes. Scale bars (b-h), 20μm. n = 5 animals per genotype. All data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. ****, p < 0.001. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test.

a-e, Cell centroid distribution of each SC cluster along the dorsal-ventral axis labeled with mWmC from all RGCs (a), αRGCs (b), ooDSGCs (c), F-RGCs (d), and T5-RGCs (e), respectively. Each box represents one mWmC+ neuron type annotated via TransA-MERFISH, and the height of each bar represents the distribution of mWmC+ cells along the dorsal-ventral axis annotated via TransA-MERFISH. The side bars indicate the overall distribution of neurons innervated by that RGC type along the dorsal-ventral axis, spanning 0-500 µm from the pial surface (y-axis). Box plots show the center and bounds of the distribution. For (a,b,d,e), n = 3 animals; for (c), n = 4 animals. f, Normalized proportions of mWmC+ cells in retino-recipient neuron types, colored by starter RGC subclass. Bars show the mean fraction of mWmC+ cells per cell type across animals. Normalized fractions were obtained using a hierarchical logistic Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM) that accounts for variation across tracing datasets, animals, tissue sections, and cell-type abundance. n = 15 biologically independent animals. Data are presented as mean ± SD.

a, Sample DIC/fluorescence images from CRACM experiments. Scale bar, 20 µm. b-c, Mapping connectivity from ooDSGCs onto Cdh7+ SC neurons using CRACM. (b) Sample EPSCs in Cdh7+ SC neurons evoked by ooDSGCs (black trace) persist in the presence of bath-applied TTX (1 µM) + 4-AP (100 µM) (blue trace) but are abolished after bath perfusion with CNQX (10 µM) + APV (50 µM) (red trace), indicating a monosynaptic excitatory connection. Blue lines indicate 2 ms period of optogenetic excitation. (c) Quantification of the average amplitudes before and after adding pharmacological blockers in ooDSGC-Cdh7+ SC connected pairs. Current amplitudes before adding any drugs are shown in black dots and bars; blue dots and bars show current amplitude after adding TTX + 4-AP; red dots and bars show current amplitude after adding CNQX + APV. Each dot represents one cell. n = 3 biologically independent animals, 8 cells, n.s. not significant. *, p = 0.0124, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. d-e, CRACM reveals a lack of monosynaptic connections from ooDSGCs onto Cbln4+ SC neurons. (d) Sample ooDSGC-evoked EPSCs have very small amplitudes (black trace) and are blocked by bath-applied TTX (1 µM) + 4-AP (100 µM) (blue trace), indicating that they are polysynaptic. Blue lines indicate 2 ms of blue LED light. (e) Quantification of the average amplitudes before and after adding pharmacological blockers in ooDSGC-Cbln4+ SC tests. Black dots and bars show current amplitudes before adding drugs; blue dots and bars show current amplitudes after adding TTX + 4-AP; red dots and bars show current amplitudes with CNQX + APV. Each dot represents one cell. n = 6 biologically independent animals, 9 cells, **, p = 0.0044, n.s. not significant. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. f-g, Lack of monosynaptic connections from all RGCs to Cbln4+ SC neurons. (f) Sample EPSCs evoked by all RGCs have small amplitudes (black trace) and are blocked by bath-applied TTX (1 µM) + 4-AP (100 µM) (blue trace), indicating that they are polysynaptic. Blue lines indicate a 2 ms period of optogenetic excitation. (g) Quantification of the average amplitudes before and after adding pharmacological blockers in all RGCs-Cbln4+ SC tests. Black dots and bars show current amplitudes before adding any drugs; blue dots and bars show current amplitudes after adding TTX + 4-AP; red dots and bars show current amplitudes with CNQX + APV. Each dot represents one cell. n = 5 biologically independent animals, 11 cells, ***, p = 0.0002, n.s., not significant. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. h-k, Retinal Cre-dependent anterograde trans-neuronal tracing from ooDSGCs to SC neurons, using AAV2-DIO-mWGA-mCherry to label SC neuronal subsets. Representative images show abundant anterograde transfer to Cdh7+ (h), but not to Cbln4+ (i) SC neurons. Quantification of mCherry+ neurons among GFP+ SC neurons is shown in (j). n = 6 animals per group; n = 214 (Cdh7), n = 237 (Cbln4) SC neurons. mCherry+ neurons among GFP+ SC neurons in the ipsilateral SC are shown in (k), mean ± s.e.m.; ****p = 1.405 × 10−10, Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. Scale bars, 50 µm. l-m, Sample images of starter cells in SC and inputs from neighboring SC neurons: Cdh7+ (l) and Cbln4+ (m) neurons in SC, showing high-efficiency overlap between Flp-dependent EGFP-2a-TVA-2a-oG (green) and RdGV: Rabies-Cherry (red). Scale bar, 40 µm. n-o, Absence of ipsilateral retinal input to the Cbln4+ neurons in the ipsilateral SC. Immunostaining of the ipsilateral retina for Satb1 (green; antibody marker for ooDSGCs), Spp1 (blue, antibody marker for alpha RGCs), and rabies-infected (red) RGCs from Cbln4+ SC neurons (n). Summary of the percentage of mCherry+ cells among SC starter neurons(o). n = 4 animals. Scale bars, 50 µm. All data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

a, AAV vector design for Cre-dependent tpCaspase3-TEV expression. b-c, Confirmation of successful reduction in retinal SACs using AAV-DIO-Caspase3-TEV in Chat-Cre by comparing SAC density in control (b) and tpCaspase3-TEV injections (c). Scale bar, 50 μm. d-e, Quantification of ablation efficiency and specificity of starburst amacrine cells (SACs) (d, n = 5 animals) compared with control saline injections (d). SAC ablation in Cbln4+ animals: **, p = 0.0026. SAC ablation in Cdh7+ animals: **, p = 0.0024. Quantification of RGC densities (n = 4 animals) after SAC ablations (e). n.s. not significant. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. f, Optomotor responses showing impaired visual acuity in SAC-ablated animals, indicating efficient elimination of SACs compared to the saline-injected group. (a-f) n = 5 animals, n.s. not significant. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. (**, green for Clbn4+ SC neurons, p = 0.007; blue for Cdh7+ SC neurons, p = 0.0026) g-i, Sample receptive field (RF) measurement for Cdh7+ SC neuron. Calcium traces of one SC neuron evoked by random dots presented at different locations on the stimulus monitor (g). Heat map of the receptive field of one SC neuron; red ellipses indicate 2D Gaussian receptive-field fits with 1-SD radii. The white cross is at the center of the receptive field. Black dots represent receptive field centers of other cells. Preferred directions of Cdh7+ SC neurons in one ROI (i). (for both h,k) Scale bar, 10 degrees. j-l, Similar to g-i but for Cbln4+ SC neurons. Calcium traces of one SC neuron (j). Heat map of the receptive field of one SC neuron (k). Preferred directions of Cbln4+ SC neurons from an imaging window of Cbln4+ SC neurons that respond strongly to upward motion collectively (l). m-n, Schematic of two-photon calcium imaging to examine the contribution of the ipsilateral eye to Cbln4+ SC neuronal responses. A black cover is placed over the ipsilateral eye of the imaged mice (m). Average (n) DSI between control (green) and ipsilateral eye covering (gray) conditions. Each dot represents one cell. n = 4 animals, 561 cells; n.s., not significant; two-sided Student’s T-test. o-p, Schematic of two-photon calcium imaging to examine the contribution of SACs in both eyes to the responses of Cbln4+ SC neurons. AAV-DIO-tpCaspase3Tev virus is injected into both eyes of the imaged mice (o). Average (p) DSI between the control (green) and both-eye SAC ablation (gray) conditions. Each dot represents one cell. n = 4 animals, 105 cells; n.s., not significant. Two-sided unpaired Student’s t-test. Efficiency of ipsilateral SAC ablation (gray) was included in (d), which was comparable to the other conditions listed above. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

Aston Villa make a mistake at the back and Lamine Yamal makes them pay inside 10 minutes ⚡ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1IcWOPMJlt

At the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

The defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back quickly from defeats.

Emery said: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

“Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

Then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

Villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

That mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

With Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

Raphinha doubles Barcelona's lead with his 18th goal of the season! 🔥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/NzFPYVzDuj

Barcelona added a third goal with Raphinha converting from close range after a sublime pass from João Cancelo.

Raphinha dedicated his goals to De Miguel, who died on Tuesday after sustaining serious injuries during a match the previous night. He said: “Tonight I don’t want to talk about football. I want to send a lot of strength to Jesus de Miguel’s family.

“May he rest in peace. In the end, this can happen to anyone. The truth is that it’s very tough. When we saw the news this morning, it was complicated. I’m incredibly shocked and sad. In the end, you go to play a match, and the same thing could happen to you. From myself, from the club, we want to send a lot of strength to his family.”

Villa did continue to fight for a consolation, with substitute Leon Goretzka heading against the post and their 3,000 travelling fans continued to sing in the rain after the final whistle.

This was the first encounter between the two clubs since the European Super Cup Final in January 1983, and yet another reminder of the upward trajectory under Emery.

This stadium will always bring back some bittersweet memories for Unai Emery, and not just because of the infamous ‘La Remontada’.

He has lost in 14 of his 15 visits here, and lost to Barcelona more times (21) than any other club in his career.

The solitary win came when he was in charge of Villarreal and one of the players in his team that night, in May 2022, was Pau Torres. He is in Villa’s back four tonight.

Since swapping Newcastle for Barcelona in the summer, the Englishman has three goals and five assists in 13 appearances in La Liga and the Champions League this season.

“I have played against them [Aston Villa] several times, and they are in good form at the moment. They are always focused and wait for their opportunities. It will be a challenge, but I am looking forward to tomorrow’s [tonight’s] game. The challenge of playing for Barca is different from anywhere else. Before, I was competing to qualify for the Champions League; now, I am competing to win every trophy.”

Unai Emery’s side will be relieved that they took a maximum nine points from their opening three games as their fixtures in this competition are getting a lot harder. This away game in Barcelona is followed up by a tricky trip to Turkey. Then it is tough back-to-back home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund.

Unai Emery has managed more than 1,100 matches but will never forget the drama of “La Remontada” as he returns to the scene on Tuesday night.

Emery is back at the Nou Camp in the Champions League for the first time since one of the most epic games in the history of the competition. While in charge of Paris St-Germain nine years ago, Emery took his team to Barcelona with a 4-0 lead from the round-of-16 first leg. Yet he was left stunned as Barcelona recovered to win the rematch 6-1, with three goals in the final seven minutes and the winner proving hugely controversial.

Sergi Roberto’s goal five minutes into added time caused a massive backlash as PSG claimed it was offside, with Emery claiming on Monday that the match showed that VAR was “necessary”.

Honking weather here in Barcelona with the rain hammering down at the Nou Camp.

It has been forecast all day and until about 5pm Spanish time it did appear that the predictions were wrong.

No such luck, however, and it is pretty torrential at the moment. Football updates to follow.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

Team news from Nou Camp to follow shortly.

#1087. Premier League identify SIX key refereeing errors in one weekend as boss Howard Webb prepares to appear in front of clubs after Arsenal blunder

Published: 06:08 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 14:15 EST, 18 November 2026

The Premier League have ruled that referees made a staggering six incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.

It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.

That is because the laws state that if a foul occurs before an offside offence, a penalty should be awarded.

Although Havertz was in an offside position, he had not committed an offence as he neither played the ball nor interfered with play.

The key match incidents panel (KMI) said: 'Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded.'

Farai Hallam's decision not to award Kai Havertz a penalty was deemed incorrect by the key match incidents panel

Coventry were wrongly denied a spot-kick in their defeat to Everton after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair

1. Everton vs Coventry City: Frank Lampard's side should have been awarded a penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

2. Everton vs Coventry City: The Toffees' second goal, scored by Thierno Barry should not have stood as the ball was adjudged to have gone into the back of the net off his hand.

3. Arsenal vs Hull City: Kai Havertz was denied a penalty after being dragged down. The referee did not award a spot-kick because Havertz in an offside position. However, that decision was incorrect, as he was not committing an offside offence and a spot-kick should therefore have been awarded.

4. Crystal Palace vs Liverpool: Palace were awarded a penalty in the last minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool after Milos Kerkez and Dario Osario clashed heads in the penalty area. The panel saw this as a natural coming together.

5. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: A penalty was given after Abdoul Ouattara tumbled over. The referee gave a foul against Lewis Cook despite Ouattara stepping across him.

6. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: Marcus Tavernier should have seen a second yellow card for time-wasting.

They did, however, praise the VAR for asking the referee to review the incident on the monitor, even though Hallam stuck with his on-field call after watching it back.

In the same weekend, Tottenham Hotspur complained to Pro Ref after Jayden Bogle's heavy challenge on Mathys Tel's ankle, which forced him off injured.

Spurs felt Bogle should have seen red, particularly after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar incident the week prior.

Reviewing the decision, the KMI panel were split but eventually concluded that the foul lacked 'the speed, force or intensity' to be considered serious foul play.

Two of the five panellists, however, felt that the challenge merited a red card.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's consolation penalty in the 92nd minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool should never have been awarded.

The KMI panel unanimously agreed the referee was wrong to award a penalty when Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio clashed heads while contesting the ball, with contact inevitable given both players were jumping.

However, VAR's decision not to intervene was supported because it was not a 'clear and obvious error'.

It is the second penalty incident in as many weeks that went against Liverpool after Alexander Isak was wrongfully denied a spot-kick against Arsenal.

On the opposite side of Merseyside, James Tarkowski was fortunate not to concede a penalty for pulling Caleb Yirenkyi's hair during Everton's win over Coventry City, with the score still 0-0 at the time. The panel found that Coventry should have been awarded a penalty while Tarkowski should have been booked.

Last season, that incident would likely have resulted in a straight red card. However, the guidance changed this term with red cards only brandished for excessive force.

Thierno Barry's goal that gave Everton the lead faced scrutiny as three panellists believed it should have been disallowed on the pitch, with the 'balance of probability suggesting the ball accidentally struck Barry's hand before directly entering the goal'.

There were also two incorrect decisions in Bournemouth's victory over Ipswich Town.

Bournemouth defender Marcus Tavernier should have been sent off for a second yellow card in the 96th minute for delaying the restart during their 2-1 win, the panel found. However, it was a close call as the panel voted 3-2 against the decision.

Ipswich's scored penalty was also deemed wrongly awarded, with Abdoul Ouattara stepping across Lewis Cook to win the spot-kick rather than being fouled by the defender.

The KMI panel consists of a representative from the Premier League and Pro Ref alongside three former managers or players and meets after every round of Premier League matches to evaluate significant refereeing decisions.

Ref boss Howard Webb will speak to Premier League clubs at a routine meeting on Thursday

While the panel is not new, this is the first season their findings have been publicly released in Pro Ref's drive for greater transparency and accountability.

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb is due to appear in front of clubs on Thursday at a routine Premier League meeting.

And in more positive news for Webb, he will be able to share that VAR delays are down this season after increasing the bar for interventions.

Meanwhile, the KMI panel have assessed 296 decisions this season - only six of which have been judged to be wrong post-VAR.

#1086. Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet

Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

“It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”

Yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

Another chance went begging when Joe Gomez fizzed a ball across the six-yard box that was screaming to be converted, but nobody could apply the finishing touch. When Trey Nyoni put Liverpool ahead, it seemed like all those local predictions of a resounding away win would come true.

Those who remember Kuyt from his Anfield days 15 years ago will recall a player who never considered any cause to be lost and the Dutchman implored his team to attack the flanks with pace, even earning himself a yellow card at one point. Eventually, the pressure paid off.

Andoni Iraola says he will not waste any more time thinking about the penalty Liverpool were denied against Arsenal and won’t seek an explanation from Pro Ref. There was a significant fallout following the 1-0 loss at Anfield on Sunday with many judges believing Stuart Attwell, who was VAR, should have consulted match official Andy Madley to highlight an obvious pull by Jurrien Timber that prevented Alexander Isak heading a Bradley Barcola cross.

Liverpool’s head coach explained in the heat of the moment that he would tell his players to go down if they felt contact in the area and Cody Gakpo, the Netherlands international, explained last night in Istanbul it was a message the squad had taken on board.

“As a team, we play pretty fair – maybe we should dive some more like the gaffer said,” Gakpo, who also had claims to be awarded a penalty against Arsenal, explained. “On both occasions you could have given a penalty or a foul, but they decided not. We have to live with the decision. That’s it.”

But as angry as he was with the situation, Iraola has drawn a line on the matter. He is not going to seek out Pro Ref for a discussion – even though he feels a number of decisions have gone against Liverpool this season – and is channelling his energy into other situations.

Iraola said: “I didn’t ask for an explanation and I haven’t received an explanation, no. I told you what you I think about the plays but, honestly, I don’t have the time to [speak to Pro Ref]. I have been preparing for Fenerbahce. It is just two days between games so I have just been focusing on this game and the opposition and how to prepare the team.”

Liverpool have made the long trip to Turkey to take on Fenerbahce on matchday four of the Champions League.

Liverpool enter this fixture having won all three Champions League matches thus far, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal to make it nine points from nine for Andoni Iraola’s side. Liverpool’s five-game unbeaten streak was ended by Arsenal in the league on Sunday. They return to the city where the club enjoyed one of their most memorable nights, beating AC Milan in the Champions League final 21 years ago.

“Istanbul is always going to be very special for Liverpool,” Iraola said. “It is difficult to find a more important night. Tomorrow [tonight] it won’t be easy, you talk about statistics, especially English teams playing here. They have very good players and a very good squad, they know how to play in this competition. We have to start strong in the game. It is very early in the season to establish comparisons. We want to continue how we have done in the Champions League, three games and nine points, it is a good chance to get to 12 points and then finish in the top eight. Champions League away is very difficult.”

In addition to the long-term absentees Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Giovanni, both Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong have missed the trip to Turkey.

Fenerbahce have made a slow start to their Champions League campaign, taking just two points from their opening three fixtures. They have drawn twice against Roma and Slavia Prague at home whilst they suffered a heavy 6-0 loss at Aston Villa. Former Liverpool forward Dirk Kuyt has been appointed their interim coach following the resignation of Ismail Kartal following their recent defeat to arch rivals Galatasaray just over a week ago.

“It is a great opportunity for us to show what we can do,” Kuyt said. “It is also a great opportunity for me, a game between two teams that are very important to me. We have a very good plan, and we have to believe in this plan. No-one who loves Fenerbahce is happy with the current situation, but this is a huge opportunity. We have players who have won the Champions League and the World Cup.”

They come into tonight’s match having lost back-to-back league games since drawing against Slavia Prague on matchday three of the Champions League. They have plenty of former Premier League players in their ranks, including Ederson, N’Golo Kante and Romelu Lukaku.

#1085. Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

#1084. Leicester City AXE controversial deal with unlicensed gambling company after sponsor sparked fan fury by appointing 'international porn star' as ambassador

Published: 14:09 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 18 November 2026

Leicester have decided to end their deal with controversial sponsors BC.GAME six months ahead of schedule.

Fans expressed fury and dismay earlier this month after the club's unlicensed gambling shirt sponsor appointed an 'international porn star' as its new ambassador.

Now Leicester have opted to conclude the partnership – in a move welcomed by supporters. A statement on Wednesday read: ‘The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward.

‘We would like to thank BC.GAME for its support throughout its two-and-a-half-year association with Leicester City and for the constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement.

‘Supporters who have purchased a BC.GAME-branded replica shirt through official LCFC retail channels within the last 28 days (since 21 October, 2026) can return it for a full refund or exchange (subject to availability) by Wednesday 2 December.’

BC.GAME, an online casino company, had been the Foxes' primary shirt sponsor since the start of the 2024-25 season. They announced a partnership with Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie in a video on X earlier this month.

Leicester City have axed a partnership with BC.GAME, after the gambling shirt sponsor appointed 'international porn star' Eva Elfie as its new ambassador

Leicester confirmed fans who have purchased a replica shirt featuring the sponsor's name within the last 28 days can return it for a full refund or exchange by December 2

Elfie, who has 4.8million Instagram followers, is known in Esports and gaming communities too

In recent years, Leicester’s spectacular decline on the pitch has mirrored the relationship with their supporters.

During the years immediately before and after their stunning Premier League triumph in 2016, it was difficult to find a club more in tune with the fanbase.

But a series of baffling decisions – including the tie-up with BC.GAME – eroded trust between the club and their supporters.

Leicester are now in League One and face a long road back but sensible moves like this one suggest they are at least facing in the right direction again.

#1083. Inside Midtjylland, the data-driven outsiders taking on Danish football’s traditional giants

Only formed in 1999, the club have used innovative thinking to become perennial title contenders – FFT headed to see them host rivals FC Copenhagen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Beneath gathering rain clouds and surrounded by thousands of hectares of windswept heathland, FourFourTwo is staring at a 33-foot statue of Vladimir Lenin.

We're not in St Petersburg or Minsk – or any former Soviet nation, for that matter – but Denmark's Jutland peninsula, as it begins to drizzle with rain. It's so wild and remote that old Vlad is one of the few faces we've seen since arriving this morning. Much like the Russian revolutionary – carved in bronze, suspended in mid-air and lying flat on his back, just like at his Moscow mausoleum – we're beginning to wonder what the hell we're doing here.

“We like to imagine that Lenin is contemplating all the terrible things he did in life,” explains Birgitte Damgaard, the proprietor of the land the statue now calls home. Birgitte's father, a local textiles tycoon and art collector, vowed to rescue the statue after watching television footage of it being toppled by Latvians during the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. “It was brought more than 500 miles – first by truck, then by ship,” she tells FFT, after we stop by for a look. “He's been lying here, staring up at the sky, for more than 30 years.”

We're a few miles outside the town of Herning, although our own reasons for being here are more straightforward – we've come to witness a football match between local side Midtjylland and league leaders FC Copenhagen. At first glance, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is a complete mismatch.

From the capital, Copenhagen are Denmark's most successful club, with a record 16 league titles. Midtjylland, meanwhile, were only founded in 1999 following the merger of two second-tier rivals, and hail from a town with fewer than 60,000 inhabitants.

Yet the latter have rapidly grown into one of the country's most formidable sides, claiming four league titles in the past 12 seasons. Last term they won the Danish Cup, and beat both Celtic and Nottingham Forest in the Europa League. When we arrive, they trail only Copenhagen in the domestic league, heading into their table-topping clash. How have they managed it all?

We wave goodbye to Lenin and Birgitte in search of answers, driving through eerily quiet farmland outside Herning, to what appears to be a bunker from 007 adventure GoldenEye. Grey and austere, the building doesn't instantly strike you as welcoming – it turns out we couldn't be more wrong.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“We call this club the miracle from out of nowhere,” beams Midtjylland's bespectacled chairman Claus Steinlein, who shakes our hand enthusiastically before welcoming us into the warmth of the club's Dream 99 training complex. “Allow us to show you why.”

Opened in 2023, Dream 99 boasts a network of pristine football pitches, as well as a spa and gym. Steinlein leads us to a mural depicting the history of the club; a collage of black and white photos resembling newspaper cutouts. It's time for a history lesson.

“Midtjylland were formed from a merger between Herning Fremad and IFS,” he explains, pointing out a photo of the day the clubs came together – the suited, smiling chairmen shaking hands. “The name honours the Jutland province.” Indeed, Midtjylland means ‘Mid-Jutland' in Danish.

“We vowed from the start to become the biggest club in Denmark,” Steinlein adds. “People told us we were crazy. We knew that if we were to prove them wrong, we'd have to be different.”

Steinlein himself saw a way to help the new club stand out. “At that time, no Danish club had its own academy,” he says. “At least not with dedicated programmes. I wanted to be the first.”

Steinlein visited the academy of French side Nantes to learn what he could, returning with a blueprint for success. He asked the board to invest a massive chunk of its fledgling budget – around €800,000 – and, to his initial shock, they agreed. There was just one problem.

“Nobody wanted to send their kids here,” laughs Steinlein. “Children here grow up wanting to play for Brondby or Copenhagen, rather than Midtjylland. Convincing people was the first battle.”

A breakthrough came via Midtjylland's own kit man, who agreed to bring his 12-year-old son with him when taking the job. “It helped that his son was Simon Kjaer,” Steinlein says. “Simon went on to make more than 100 appearances for Denmark.”

Kjaer made a handful of first-team showings after graduating from the academy in 2007, before being sold to Palermo for €4m – a huge sum for a young Dane at the time. Steinlein's academy received a huge financial and reputational boost. “That gave our project the lift-off it needed,” he says.

Midtjylland began painstakingly forming partnerships across the region, more than 100 amateur sides regularly sending their best and brightest for trials. In exchange, Midtjylland provide equipment and tickets to first-team games. “It's about inspiring the next generation,” adds Steinlein.

Neither are Midtjylland's operations limited to the best Danish talent. We're led into an office to meet Jonas Dal, who heads the club's Nigerian academy.

“Every year, more than seven million children are born in Nigeria, compared with about 50,000 here, so the pool of talent is naturally much larger,” says Dal, who was once held at gunpoint during a visit to Lagos, but plays a key role in the Midtjylland project. “We bring over the most promising players. We have to be patient with them, because the weather and culture in Denmark are all very new to them.”

Right on cue, we meet Rilwan Hassan, who joined Midtjylland from the Lagos academy in 2010, before spending close to a decade playing for the club. He's now a coach with the academy. “It was so cold,” he recalls of his arrival as a teen. “But it was a massive opportunity. I was going into the unknown, but I quickly found out that this club was striving to be the very best. Everybody was pulling in the same direction.”

Many of Midtjylland's academy products, either from Nigeria or closer to home, are lured to the club with the promise they'll be sold if a bigger side comes in for them. Indeed, selling players has become a key aspect of Midtjylland's model. “If Liverpool or Barcelona come in for one of our players, that's perfect,” says Steinlein. “It means they've performed well and we can profit. Everybody wins.”

Following their formation, Midtjylland were immediately promoted to the top flight, before cementing themselves as consistent top-five finishers. Yet while results and youth development were impressive, they were beginning to struggle financially. Player sales barely covered the growing cost of operations, especially with European qualification hardly guaranteed each season.

“We'd wanted to become the biggest and best team in Denmark, but we were still some way off that,” winces Steinlein. “That soon changed, though.” The man who would help them take that next step was an Englishman with a physics degree, already making a name for himself at Brentford.

In June 2012, Matthew Benham had taken control of the Bees, then in League One, having made millions as the impresario of Smartodds – a company providing statistical analysis on sporting events to professional gamblers. That data also gave Benham extraordinary insight into how football games are won and lost, where and how goals are most often scored, and which players were being undervalued by the market. In short, a recipe for success.

That same year also saw Benham invite a Danish author to give a presentation to his staff. Benham had become fascinated by Rasmus Ankersen's book The Gold Mine Effect, which looked into cultural anomalies, such as why Jamaica consistently produces the best sprinters. Ankersen was equally impressed with Benham.

“At the time, Brentford were third in League One, and there were a couple of games to go,” the Dane would later recall. “I said to him, ‘What are the chances of you guys getting promoted?' When you ask that question, you expect an emotional yes or no, but he just said, ‘There's a 42.3 per cent chance.' That was when I knew he was a guy who was thinking very differently.”

Benham and Ankersen, the latter a promising player at Midtjylland before injury sent him down a different path, became firm friends. In 2014, the Dane convinced the data guru to invest in a second football club, with Benham paying £6.2m for a majority stake in Midtjylland. He brought with him his legion of statisticians, sports scientists and coaches. It was about to go turbo.

“This club now has tools to evaluate teams and players with much more accuracy using data,” said Ankersen, who was swiftly installed as chairman by Benham. “The model we're using could be applied in any country.”

Midtjylland's strategy was transformed overnight. “Set-pieces then became a fundamental part of the way we played,” Steinlein tells us on the balcony of the training complex, which overlooks the first-team's pitches. “They still are. We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes. The approach has been successful.”

In Benham's first year, Midtjylland were crowned Danish champions; their first major trophy. The team finished with a goal difference of plus 15 from set-pieces. “We were finally the best club in Denmark,” grins Steinlein. “A dream come true. Benham's stats and our focus on set-pieces were key.”

We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes

Next, Steinlein leads us into the main communal area of Dream 99. Above the only coffee machine in the building, where footfall is at its highest, a chart denoting Midtjylland's historical success from set-pieces adorns the wall. The 2015, 2018, 2020, 2024 and 2025 campaigns are highlighted as being particularly prolific – the Wolves won the league four out of five of those years.

“That one time we didn't win the title still bothers us,” laughs Steinlein. “We want our players and staff to be hurt by that, too. Topping this chart needs to be their motivation.”

Benham sold his stake in Midtjylland in 2023 to better focus on Brentford, though the two sides retain a close partnership. Today the club is owned by fashion tycoon Anders Holch Povlsen, Denmark's richest person, with an estimated worth of more than £12bn.

Ankersen has also departed, though his influence is still felt. A school called Guldminen, named after his book, was built into the Dream 99 complex. It aims to nurture both the best young sporting and academic talent in Denmark. FFT learns that students are given free rein of the building, meaning it isn't unusual for first-team players and schoolkids to share meals.

“We have a word for the environment we've fostered here: ‘sammenhold,'” says Steinlein. “It literally translates to ‘unity club', but it means so much more than that. It's about every person, from the kids to the first-teamers, coaches and cleaners, feeling part of something bigger. We are one entity. That's what sammenhold is, and it's our way of life.”

Overwhelmed by the scale and passion behind the Midtjylland project, FFT waves goodbye to the dream factory and makes our way over to the MCH Arena for tonight's crucial showdown against FC Copenhagen.

Inside the 12,000-capacity stadium, opened in 2004, FFT catch up with fans who are noisily drinking beer out of plastic cups and watching Brondby's early fixture on a big screen. Ahead of kick-off, we chat to lifelong Midtjylland fan Thomas Schouv Jacobsen. “My father is from Ikast, one of the two clubs that merged into Midtjylland,” he says. “Supporting this club since the start has been an extraordinary ride. The jump from winning a few silver medals to actually taking our first ever title in 2015 was indescribable. Seeing my father's face when we scored the decisive goal in the decisive match against Copenhagen is something that I'll never forget.”

Midtjylland's record against title rivals Copenhagen is certainly impressive.

Going into this game, the latter have won just twice in their past 14 meetings, with Midtjylland winning seven. Tonight, however, there's a fear that the league leaders might be too strong, especially given that regular Midtjylland defenders Rasmus Kristensen, Magnus Jensen and Martin Erlic are all out injured.

“We've had terrible setbacks in defence this season,” Jacobsen laments. “But, come May, we should have a very good chance of taking the championship. I think we have the best squad and the ability to come out successful.”

FFT also catches a moment with a Copenhagen fan. “We're massively important to Danish football because we have the biggest fanbase and play European football every year,” says lifelong supporter Kevin Willendrup.

“We're the flagship club. Our games against Brondby are by far the biggest in Denmark. There isn't the same level of hatred between the Midtjylland and Copenhagen fanbases – they've become extremely good in a very short space of time. Along with us, they're favourites to win the league every season. It's great that another team has emerged with so much quality.”

Yet there's no doubt in Willendrup's mind who'll emerge victorious tonight. “Copenhagen will win here for the first time in a long time,” he says. “We're on an incredible run under Bo Svensson and we're starting to look like a championship-winning team.”

As fans around us drain their beers and head inside, FFT does the same. We emerge onto the terraces to a magnificent sight. It's a record crowd, as flags swirl from the melee behind either end of the field. To our right, the home fans bellow into the evening sky and beat war drums. Off to our left, the white-clad Copenhagen fans are making their own thunderous racket.

Pitchside for the warm-ups, we see some familiar faces, including former Bournemouth beanpole Philip Billing, now at Midtjylland, and the ex-Cardiff targetman Andreas Cornelius, who is among the visitors' line-up. Curiously, Midtjylland's warm-up routine involves pain-staking set-piece practice; coaches repeatedly whipping vicious free-kicks into a packed box of giants.

As the players head inside to make their final preparations, we brush past former Everton and Real Madrid hard man Thomas Gravesen, who has presumably been loaned to a Danish TV outlet by the poker tables of Las Vegas. “Should be a good night tonight, guys,” he winks. “This is one of the biggest games of the season.”

The players emerge before kick-off to a deafening roar – the tifos, flags and rhythmic beating of drums providing an epic backdrop – before getting the game underway beneath the floodlights.

Copenhagen swiftly take charge but their dominance doesn't last. In the 12th minute, Midtjylland win a free-kick high on the left, not far from the corner flag. As Billing fizzes it in, FFT remarks that it's silly he isn't in the box himself given his size. He quickly shows us what we know, planting a ball squarely on to the head of onrushing Nigerian forward Friday Etim, whose effort crashes into the net to make it 1-0. Recorded wolf howls are played over the PA system as the roof comes off the MCH Arena.

Copenhagen dust themselves down and settle back into their rhythm, knocking the ball around menacingly, but they're unable to find a way through as Midtjylland's makeshift defence, marshalled by the imperious Andreas Maxso, clear everything.

Such low-block defending inevitably leads to mistakes, however, and one arrives just after the break, as wing-back Kjell Watjen fells Copenhagen skipper Thomas Delaney just inside the penalty area. The referee points to the spot and former Southampton star Mohamed Elyounoussi slots in an equaliser. The Copenhagen fans go wild.

The visitors take their possession up a notch. Robert Silva slaloms down the left and into the Midtjylland box, but his cutback is prodded away before the rebound is fired wide. Surely it's just a matter of time before they score again.

Then the unthinkable happens for the league leaders in the 62nd minute. Under very little pressure, Copenhagen goalkeeper Diant Ramaj passes straight to opponent Etim, who rounds the shot-stopper and shapes to pull the trigger, only to find his path blocked by recovering defenders.

As an entire stadium holds its breath, Etim squares the ball to Denil Castillo, arriving in support. The Ecuadorian fires low and hard into the Copenhagen net, and Midtjylland are in the lead once more, courtesy of a horrific error. Clearly shaken, Copenhagen never recover their rhythm. When the final whistle blows half an hour later, it's pure ecstasy for the Wolves supporters.

FFT rush onto the field to join the Midtjylland players as they celebrate in front of the frenzied home end. Arm in arm, players and coaches bounce in front of the melee, as we grab a word with Billing. “It's amazing when a result like this comes off,” he yells above the bedlam, with a huge smile on his face.

“We knew they'd play nice football, but that we could win it with our set plays and our physicality. We had to cope with a lot of injuries today, so the fact we came out of this game with a win is massive for us.”

When the players are finally separated from their adoring public, we're invited to join them inside. The dressing room is packed as victorious manager Mike Tullberg delivers a rousing speech in front of players, board members, staff and children. This must be what Steinlein meant by sammenhold. “I'm proud of you today, guys,” he says, singling out Maxso and his fellow defenders for an extraordinary performance. “There's a long way to go but we've given our ambitions a huge boost.”

A post shared by FourFourTwo (@fourfourtwouk)

Castillo, scorer of the winning goal, is also singled out in surprising fashion by the boss. “You've recently surpassed 100 games for us and what a way to cap it off,” Tullberg enthuses. “You keep playing like that and you won't be here for another 100.”

The whole room then erupts into an obscure song – a tradition that also sees players dancing and banging their lockers to the beat (watch the video above). It's a joyous scene. Afterwards, we head into chairman Steinlein's personal office, resembling a wood-panelled smoking room. The likes of Kenny Dalglish and Louis van Gaal have been guests here before us.

Drinks begin flowing and, at some point, FFT is only vaguely aware that the night is coming to an end. When we finally head back out into the cold Scandinavian air, it's with a sense that we've witnessed something truly spectacular – a wonder from nowhere.

With this result, there are just two points between Denmark's leading sides – one of them a traditional giant from an illustrious European city, the other a motley crew of dreamers and disrupters who refuse to accept the status quo.

It's the sort of revolution Vladimir Lenin, now lying flat on his back on a rain-soaked heath in our rear-view mirror, might have approved of.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

#1082. Gold for the West Bank: Meet Palestinian karate champ Mariam Bsharat

The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.

"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."

Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.

"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.

Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."

That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.

"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.

"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."

The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

#1081. Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague

With a stylish assist and a gorgeous goal, Viktor Gyokeres produced the sort of match-winning performance that suggests the Swedish striker is making significant progress at last. It has not always been straightforward for him at Arsenal, but this was unquestionably one of his better showings, and it continued an encouraging upturn in his form.

Gyokeres has been the second-choice striker for most of this season, with Mikel Arteta usually preferring the more subtle Kai Havertz in attack. There are signs, though, that Gyokeres is now growing in belief. Following this victory over Slavia Prague, which was much more narrow and nervy than it should have been, he has now scored two goals and registered three assists in his last five appearances.

Even more promising than those statistics was his all-round play in Prague. In the first half especially, Gyokeres held on to long passes, combined with his team-mates and tested the opposition with his runs in behind. For Arsenal’s first goal, he found Noni Madueke with a brilliant pass. For their second, he curled a fabulous strike into the top corner.

“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.
